A scene built with arguments besides options (Clockwork Keep's next floor carries the score and lives) returns them from replay_arguments() , as they were when it was built; they must read back from JSON exactly as returned: class FloorScene ( Scene ): def __init__ ( self , floor_index = 0 , player_score = 0 , options = None , groups = None ): super () . __init__ ( options = options , groups = groups ) # first: the start capture begins here self . floor_index = floor_index self . starting_player_score = player_score def replay_arguments ( self ): return { 'floor_index' : self . floor_index , 'player_score' : self . starting_player_score } Draw random numbers only after super().__init__() : the capture begins there. Replay ( --replay-trace PATH ) # At startup the replay reads the recording, applies its recorded options and seeds the random streams with its seed. It refuses, logging the reason and exiting with one of the exit codes , when: the recording is of another game, cannot be read (not gzip, no permission, a directory) or has an unsupported format version: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65); the file does not exist: MISSING_INPUT (66); --record-trace is given too: OPTIONS_REFUSED (64). Recording over a replay is what --rebaseline does, and only it. A recording made by a different engine version replays with one warning. A version-2 recording replays with one warning too: it has no input snapshots, so polled input reads as idle. Each frame, the replay serves the recorded events, dt , input, devices, saves and clocks. Then it compares the frame with the recording: the active scene's class, then each recorded sprite in draw order (present, rect , visible ), along with the frame's internal events, control events and pump count. The first difference stops a headless replay, as does the last recorded frame; a watched replay pauses there instead. Closing the window stops any replay. Then it reports how it went (logged, or printed to stdout under --headless ). A sprite divergence lists that sprite in the last 20 frames up to the divergent one, as recorded and as replayed: Replay diverged at frame 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16] Ball#2, last 20 frames (expected | got): 6100: [400, 290, 16, 16] visible | [400, 290, 16, 16] visible ... 6120: [412, 300, 16, 16] visible | [412, 301, 16, 16] visible Other divergences (the scene, an event, the frame or pump count) are reported on their one line. A replay that matched reports Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording) (or (quit before the end) , when the window was closed or a watched replay's viewer pressed Esc), and one that matched up to the cut-off of a truncated recording Replay ended early at frame 4312: the recording is truncated . Every replay that ends normally, watched or headless, exits with its result: SUCCESS (0) when it matched or was quit before the end, REPLAY_DIVERGED (1) when it diverged, UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) for a truncated recording. A crash, Ctrl-C, a signal or the game's own exit ends the run as for any run, and the report then says only where the replay stopped ( Replay stopped at frame 12: the run ended with INTERNAL_ERROR (70) ); if the replay had already reached its result, the report gives it, then then the run ended with ... (see exit codes ). The game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) ) before the replay reached its result exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), never SUCCESS , which would say it matched (a rebaseline takes it as the game ending early instead: below). A recording whose header or first frame cannot be decoded (a malformed device, saves or input field) is refused as unusable ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , 65), like an unreadable file. While a replay runs, real keyboard, mouse, touch, joystick, controller, device and window events are blocked at SDL, so they never reach the game (a watched replay leaves key presses and releases unblocked for its controls, which never pass them on to the game). The block is applied again on every pump (event managers created mid-run allow their types again). Each type's earlier blocked state is restored exactly when the replay ends, normally or after an error. QUIT, the window's close event and custom event types are never blocked, so closing the window still ends the replay. Blocking also refuses posts of those types: game code that fakes input by posting KEYDOWN loses the post, which shows up as a missing internal event divergence. A watched replay leaves KEYDOWN and KEYUP unblocked, so such a post arrives there and matches its recording: a recording of a game that posts keys can match watched and diverge headless (and under --audit ). Recorded window references in events are served as None , as live events of the display window carry. Watching a replay # A replay without --headless is watched: a read-only game inside a game ( glitchygames/replay/viewer.py ). The outer loop, the replay viewer, owns the window: it ticks 60 times a second of real time whatever the speed and whether paused, reads the viewer's keys, and presents the recorded game's latest frame with the status bar drawn on it. The inner loop, the recorded game, runs its frames in full (logic, update and render) at their recorded frame times: each tick runs as many as the real time since the last tick, times the speed, pays for (at most MAX_INNER_FRAMES_PER_TICK , and only within an 11 ms real-time budget per tick, so keys and drawing keep their 60 Hz). It never owes more than one tick's worth: after a stall it runs one bounded burst and drops the rest, and when the recorded game cannot keep up with the speed the status bar says so and shows the real speed ( can't keep up: ×3.2 ). So 1x shows about one recorded frame per tick, 8x about eight, ¼x one every fourth tick. Which frames run when never changes what they do, so a watched replay is exactly as exact as a headless one. It first runs frame 0, then holds on a start screen: that frame dimmed, "Press Spacebar to Start Game Replay" centred, and a smaller line naming the debug overlay's keys ( F3: debug overlay F4: next panel ). Frame 0's sounds play before Space, and a one-frame recording reaches its end at the start screen. The screen is drawn by the pause screen's MessageScreen ( glitchygames/ui/message_screen.py ) with its own message and look, as an overlay on the presented frame: switching to a real pause scene would change the recorded scene sequence. Nothing runs while the replay is held: no frame, no frame clock, no recorded input. The viewer's keys go to the replay's controls ( glitchygames/replay/controls.py ), never to the game. Each key acts once per press (the key repeat games turn on is ignored); . and , held act once, then after 300 ms ten times a second: Key Action Space Start the replay from the start screen, then pause or resume . While paused, run one frame , While paused, step back one frame (held: one more frame back per repeat, restarting once on release) Home Restart at the beginning, paused after frame 0 D Restart just before the divergence, once the replay has found one ] / [ Double or halve the playback speed (0.25 to 8) B Bookmark the frame shown in the status bar S Save a copy of the recording with the bookmarks as breakpoints Esc Quit the replay F3 / F4 Toggle the debug overlay / show its next panel A status bar at the bottom centre shows frame 6120 / 9800 · 1:42.0 · ×1 · paused · diverged at 6120 (the parts that apply), drawn on the presented frame after the debug overlay, so it is never in a screenshot or a trace. At a divergence or the end of the recording the replay pauses with the debug overlay on and a banner above the status bar ( Diverged at frame 6120: ... or End of recording ); stepping past the end does nothing, and Esc ends the run with the replay's result. Step back, Home and D # A replay cannot run backwards, and the engine cannot be rebuilt in-process, so these keys restart the replay in a fresh process ( glitchygames/replay/rebuild.py ) with the same command line (every option kept, --replay-fps included) plus --replay-pause-at-frame N , an explicit --debug-overlay or --no-debug-overlay , and the viewer's speed, debug panel and the divergence found so far ( --replay-viewer-state , internal; D works at once after a restart). The window closes and a new one opens; the end-of-run performance reports wait for the last replay. The restarted replay skips the start screen and rebuilds: frames 0 to N - 1 run in full, unpresented and unpaced, in silence (each frame's sounds are stopped after it and music is paused until the rebuild ends, unless the game paused it itself), with Rebuilding: frame k / N shown on a cleared window every 0.1 s and printed every second (Esc still quits). It then pauses with frame N next, showing frame N - 1's picture; frame 0 always runs, so Home pauses after it. The first replay process supervises the restarts: each later replay that steps back hands its restart command to it ( --replay-restart-handoff , internal) instead of starting a process of its own, so there are never more than two (the supervisor keeps the memory its own replay used). The run exits with the last replay's status, but REPLAY_DIVERGED once any of the runs diverged; SIGTERM or SIGHUP to the supervisor ends the child too (killed with SIGKILL, without its teardown: a replay never records, so nothing is lost). Stepping back from far into a long recording takes as long as rebuilding up to there. --replay-pause-at-frame is ignored with --headless (nothing could unpause the replay). Bookmarks (B and S) # B bookmarks the frame the status bar shows ( frame N : paused with frame N next). S writes a copy of the recording next to it, x.bookmarked.jsonl.gz for x.jsonl.gz , with a {"kind": "breakpoint", "label": "bookmark"} control event added to frame N - 1 (the frame whose picture was shown) for each bookmark, and logs where. With no bookmarks it writes nothing and says no bookmarks to save . Saving the same bookmarks again writes nothing ( bookmarks already saved to ... ), unless that copy was deleted since. A copy an earlier session saved from the same recording keeps its bookmarks: a new save adds to them. A file of that name that is a copy of another recording is never written over. The copy's header names its source ( bookmarked_copy_of ), and only a file with that field is ever updated in place. The original recording is never written, even one you named something.bookmarked.jsonl.gz yourself; its copy is something.bookmarked.bookmarked.jsonl.gz . The copy is written aside and then moved into place. The copy replays exactly like its source, headless included: Breakpoints are applied again on their frame and never compared. A truncated source's copy is marked source_truncated , so it still ends as truncated ( UNUSABLE_INPUT headless, the truncated banner when watched). A version-2 source's copy is marked input_capture_format_version: 2 , so it keeps the version-2 input warning and does not compare control events. A watched replay of the copy pauses at each breakpoint, showing frame N again with breakpoint: bookmark . A rebuild after a restart runs past breakpoints to its own pause frame. Stepping back (or Home, or D) with bookmarks saves the copy first and restarts on the copy, so bookmarks survive restarts. In the restarted replay: The bookmark list starts with the copy's bookmarks, so S keeps them. Playing forward pauses at every earlier bookmark again. If the copy cannot be saved, the restart uses the recording it was replaying and logs a warning naming the bookmarks lost. --replay-fps {recorded,real} # With recorded (the default), FPS events, the performance statistics and the debug overlay's performance panel use the recorded frame times, and FPS events are compared exactly. With real , they use this machine's measured frame times and FPS events are not compared; sprites that draw the FPS value may then diverge. Logic always receives the recorded dt . Headless runs ( --headless ) # --headless runs any game on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers: no window and no sound. It sets SDL_VIDEODRIVER and SDL_AUDIODRIVER to dummy as soon as the options are read, before pygame starts its display and mixer. If pygame was already started before the engine (by code run at import), a display or mixer on another driver is restarted on the dummy one, with a warning. A live headless run is paced to the target FPS as usual (an unpaced live frame would last about a millisecond of game time) and ends however the game ends. A headless replay is not paced at all, since its frame times come from the recording, never waits (no start screen, no pause at a divergence or the end; its key events stay blocked), prints its report to stdout instead of logging it, and exits with its result as above. The determinism audit ( --audit ) # --replay-trace PATH --audit does not replay in-process. It runs the same command again, with --headless added, as two child processes, with PYTHONHASHSEED set to 1 and 2, and each child writes a SHA-256 digest of every replayed frame. The audit passes (exit SUCCESS , 0) when both runs match the recording and their digests match each other; otherwise it reports the first differing frame and exits AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC (3). A child that cannot start, hangs, crashes (exits with any status but 0, or 1 with a recorded divergence) or writes no digests means the audit could not run: INTERNAL_ERROR (70). Fresh processes and different hash seeds make set and dict ordering bugs show up. The audit compares only what the replay samples: the scene class and each sprite's rect , visible and draw order. Pixels, audio and game state that never moves, hides or reorders a sprite are not compared. It is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) with --replay-fps real , under python -E or -I (which would keep PYTHONHASHSEED from reaching the children) and without --replay-trace . A truncated recording is refused before the children start ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , 65): an audit needs the whole recording. Exit codes # The exit code alone says who refused the run and why. Every code is a member of glitchygames.exit_codes.ExitCode (also importable from glitchygames.engine ); the engine logs the code it exits with as Exiting with OPTIONS_REFUSED (64) . Code ExitCode member Meaning 0 SUCCESS Success; the replay matched; the audit is deterministic; the rebaseline was written 1 REPLAY_DIVERGED A replay's frames differ from the recording 2 ARGUMENT_PARSER_ERROR A usage error from argparse; the engine never exits with it itself 3 AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC --audit 's two runs differ from each other or from the recording 4 GENERATION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's generation request 5 EXTRACTION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's frame extraction 6 AUDIO_DROPOUT_RISK scripts/audio_glitch_probe.py found a risk of audio dropouts 7 REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST --rebaseline wrote NEW, but the run never received some of OLD's input (it ended early, or did not pump a recorded batch) 8 PROCESSING_SLOWER A replay matched, but its processing time exceeded the recording's by more than --max-processing-slowdown 64 OPTIONS_REFUSED The engine refuses the options given (a combination it will not run) 65 UNUSABLE_INPUT The recording or input data is unusable (another game's recording, an unsupported format version, a corrupt or unreadable file, a bad server response) 66 MISSING_INPUT The input file does not exist 69 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE A required service (the API server) cannot be reached 70 INTERNAL_ERROR An uncaught exception during a run or its teardown (logged with its traceback, after the teardown), or an audit that could not run 73 CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT An output file or directory cannot be created or written (a rebaseline's new recording could not be moved into place) 129 HANGUP Stopped by SIGHUP (Unix only) 130 INTERRUPTED Stopped by SIGINT (Ctrl-C) 143 TERMINATED Stopped by SIGTERM 149 BREAK Stopped by SIGBREAK (Windows only: Ctrl-Break) 0, 64-70 and 73 have the values of BSD sysexits.h (Python's os.EX_OK , os.EX_USAGE and so on, which exist only on Unix, so the values are defined in the engine). The signal codes are 128 + the signal number. A run stopped by one of those signals exits only after the normal teardown, so a recording is complete: the engine handles SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGBREAK for the whole run (unless the game installed its own handler) and turns off SDL's own signal handling ( SDL_NO_SIGNAL_HANDLERS ), which would otherwise turn SIGINT and SIGTERM into a QUIT event. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, Python ignores SIGPIPE, and SIGQUIT keeps its core-dump convention. An engine started off the main thread cannot install its handlers, so SIGTERM then ends it the system's default way, without the teardown. An exception raised before the run starts (while the engine is being constructed) exits with Python's default status 1. Comparing processing time ( --compare-processing ) # A recording holds each frame's processing time ( processing_seconds ): the frame's work (logic, events, frame services, positioning and rendering), without presenting it, without the recorder's own writing and without the pacing sleep. The header's latest measurement run ( measurement_runs[0] , see "Content hashes and measurement history" below) names the machine it was measured on (system, version and architecture, never the host name). These are diagnostics: a replay never compares them with the recording to decide whether it matched, and never serves them to the game. The comparison uses the newest entry, processing_seconds[0] . --replay-trace PATH --headless --compare-processing measures this machine's processing time for every replayed frame the same way and prints one line after the replay's report: Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording) Processing: the replay took 14.2% longer than the recording (9800 frames: 30.410 s against 26.630 s; median frame 3.100 ms against 2.710 ms); slowest against the recording: frame 812 +6.100 ms, frame 813 +5.920 ms, frame 4400 +3.010 ms --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT (which implies --compare-processing ) makes it a check: a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer in total exits PROCESSING_SLOWER (8). A divergence still exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), and a recording without processing times (made before they were recorded) cannot be checked: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65), with Processing: nothing to compare after the report. Why processing time and not wall-clock time: a live run is paced (most of each frame is the sleep before the next) and a headless replay is not paced at all, so their total times measure different things. Processing time measures the same work in both. It only compares on the same machine, so make the baseline on the machine that will check it (a CI runner); the report says so when the recording names another machine. Pacing still slows the work itself: between paced frames the processor idles and clocks down, so a live recording's frames take longer than the same frames in an unpaced replay (one Clockwork Keep session measured about 65% faster replayed than recorded live). So make the baseline with a rebaseline, which is measured unpaced as every later replay is, and check against it: # Once, on the CI machine: the baseline (the same inputs, measured unpaced) uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --rebaseline baseline.jsonl.gz --headless # On every change: fail if the work got more than 10% slower uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace baseline.jsonl.gz --headless --max-processing-slowdown 10 Replays of the same session against such a baseline land within about 1% of it. The latest measurement run says whether it paced its frames ( processing_paced ; a live run with a target FPS, as recording began) and names its frame-pacing timer, paced or not ( pacing_timer : the timer backend, its final spin and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did; glitchygames/timing.py ), and the report adds a note when the baseline was paced. --compare-processing needs --headless (a watched replay presents, steps and rebuilds frames as its viewer asks) and is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) with --audit and with --rebaseline (a rebaseline's NEW records the current code's own processing times anyway). The contract is glitchygames/replay/processing.py 's docstring. Content hashes and measurement history # Every frame a recorder writes carries two histories, newest first, and the header a third (design: plans/2026-10-20-recording-content-hash-and-history.md ; contract: glitchygames/recording_history.py ): Where Field Each entry Depth constant (10) frame content_hash the frame's content hash CONTENT_HASH_HISTORY_DEPTH frame processing_seconds its processing time ( null when not measured) PROCESSING_SECONDS_HISTORY_DEPTH header measurement_runs the run's provenance: machine, processing_paced , pacing_timer (its frame-pacing timer, paced or not: backend, final spin, and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did), engine, pygame and Python versions, measured_at , rebaselined_from , hash_scheme , and frame_count (how many frames it wrote; filled in when the next rebaseline stacks onto it, null for the newest run, whose count is the file's) MEASUREMENT_RUNS_HISTORY_DEPTH A fresh recording writes one entry in each. A rebaseline puts its own in front of the replayed recording's and drops the oldest past the depth, so index i means run i in every list. If the runs' depth is tuned below the hash depth, the deeper hashes have no run, so no hash_scheme : treat their scheme as unknown. A reader takes the fields of a run it knows and ignores fields a newer engine added. The content hash is the first 64 bits of SHA-256 of the frame's content fields as a JSON reader decodes them (string keys, lists), encoded as compact, key-sorted JSON (hash scheme 1), so the stored hash is the one a reader recomputes from the frame it reads. Content is everything the game did or took in: dt , the event batches, input, control events, devices, saves, scene starts, the scene and its sprites. Measurements (the two history fields) are left out. Every frame field is one or the other, and the hash refuses a field that is neither, so a new field cannot slip in or out unnoticed. A rebaseline copies the inputs, dt included, so an unchanged game gives the same hash one entry deeper, and a changed one shows exactly which frames changed. Two fresh recordings of the same script differ anyway (each measures its own dt , and the game moves by it). A recording's own hash, for any run, is derived from its frames' hashes: recording_content_hash(frames=..., run_index=i) ; it is not stored. Neither history is compared by a replay or served to the game. They are the record the baselines in the repository keep: behaviour (hashes) and speed (processing times) over time. Golden replays # tests/fixtures/replays/<game>/golden.jsonl.gz holds a recorded session of each example game (PaddleSlap, Clockwork Keep and both Brave Adventurer editions). scripts/record_scripted_session.py recorded them through the real engine loop, with a supervisor posting each game's golden input script. Each recording is a test item of its own: the pytest plugin glitchygames/testing/replays.py (loaded by the root conftest.py ) collects every .../fixtures/replays/<console-script>/<name>.jsonl.gz as <console-script>/<name> , replays it headless in a child process through the console script's entry point ( --replay-trace PATH --headless ) and fails, with the exit code and the child's output (the divergence report), unless it exits ExitCode.SUCCESS . A directory that is not a console script is a collection error. Another project's games can use the plugin the same way ( pytest_plugins = ['glitchygames.testing.replays'] ). Re-record a fixture only deliberately, after finding out why it stopped replaying; the commands are in the script's docstring. After an intentional change, rebaseline it instead (below), so it keeps its recorded inputs. Rebaselining ( --rebaseline NEW ) # --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless replays OLD's inputs on the current code and writes what that code did to NEW: the same inputs and a new picture. The contract is glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py 's docstring. The replay does not stop at a divergence: it runs to OLD's last frame (or until the game ends), counting every frame that differs and naming every sprite that differs in them. NEW holds OLD's inputs as the replay served them: the event batches with their origins (code-posted events stay internal , so replaying NEW delivers nothing twice), dt , input_changes , re-applied control events, and each frame's saves_opened , devices_opened and device_enumeration copied from OLD. Its sprites and markers are the current code's. Its header is OLD's (seed, start time, options, saves, devices) with rebaselined_from naming OLD and this run's engine, pygame and Python versions. A cut-off (truncated) OLD gives NEW source_truncated : NEW ends as truncated too, so its replay exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) at the cut-off, --audit refuses it, and it cannot be a golden fixture (the plugin expects SUCCESS ). Rebaseline a complete recording for those. A version-2 OLD (no input snapshots) gives an honest format-3 NEW: its polled input is the idle input the replay served, recorded as such, and its markers are compared when NEW is replayed (OLD's were not). Input OLD has that the run never received is not moved anywhere else (that would invent an input sequence OLD does not have); it is reported. That is the external events of batches a frame did not pump (the current code pumped fewer times than recorded), and OLD's frames after the game ended early. NEW is written to NEW.partial and moved into place only when the run ends normally; a run that crashes, is interrupted or fails its own exit ( sys.exit(1) ) writes nothing; the game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) ) ends it early as quit_game() does (NEW holds the frames that ran, exit REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST ). If the move fails (say NEW is a directory), the finished NEW.partial is kept, its path logged and printed, and the run exits CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73). NEW is never OLD, and NEW.partial is never OLD either. A NEW.partial that cannot be written at all is refused before the replay starts, with one line and CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73), as is an unwritable --record-trace or --replay-digest file. NEW is an original, never a bookmarked copy (OLD's bookmarked_copy_of is dropped), so S on a replay of NEW never rewrites it. It prints one line to stdout and exits SUCCESS (0), however many frames differ: Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: 412 frames differ (first at 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16]); sprites affected: Ball#2, Ball#3 or Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: no frames differ . Lost input (above) is added to the line and logged as a warning, e.g. ; 3 recorded input events not delivered (first at frame 812); ended at frame 500 of 9800 . NEW is still written (it replays clean), but the run exits REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST (7) instead, so a script that replaces fixtures notices that NEW is not a faithful re-run of OLD's session. It is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) without --replay-trace or without --headless (a watched replay holds frames and takes the viewer's keys, so it is refused rather than made headless quietly), when NEW or NEW.partial is OLD's file, and with --record-trace , --audit , --replay-digest (the audit's tools; a rebaseline is not audited) or --replay-fps real (FPS events from this machine's frame times would become the baseline). An unusable OLD is refused like any replay ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , MISSING_INPUT ). NEW replays on the current code with no divergence when the rebaseline replayed all of OLD: a truncated OLD gives a truncated NEW, whose replay matches up to its cut-off and exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) like any truncated recording. Replacing a golden fixture with it stays a deliberate, reviewed step: read the summary, check the change is the intended one, then move NEW over the fixture yourself. In-game playback # A running game can play a recording to a rebuilt scene and then go on: attract-mode demos, instant replays and ghosts. Demos and instant replays run in a playback scope , not a new engine run ( glitchygames/replay/playback.py 's docstring is the contract): the scene is rebuilt from its start (see Scene starts above) on scoped doors that serve the recording, the live scene is stashed untouched, saves are a sandbox, the random streams, clocks and FPS timer are put back afterwards, and the live game's own posts and the player's releases, device and window events are held and handed back when the scope ends. A --record-trace session that plays a scope records it, and replays it exactly. An error inside the scope ends the scope (logged) and the live game goes on. scene_manager.last_playback_outcome says how the last scope ended (its kind, reason and frames played). What belongs to the scope ends with it: supervisors and control event handlers its scene adds (in setup() , cleanup() or an event handler; a live supervisor's additions stay), and the playback scene's own events still queued when it ends (posted in update() or an event handler after its last pump: the live game never receives them, so a goal posted there cannot start a second instant replay). What the live game's own supervisors and handlers post while it plays stays the live game's: a supervisor that calls end_playback() and then posts an event has it delivered to the live game after the scope. A playback never rumbles the player's controllers, and the live scene's synth voices (and those of the game behind a pause screen the instant replay began from) pause behind it and play on after. Inside a scope, a replay of the session still applies the session's breakpoints (a bookmark on a frame a demo played pauses there); the played recording's own breakpoints are never applied again. A --record-trace recording of a session that played a scope replays exactly, but cannot itself be played in-game from a frame inside or after that scope (only an instant-replay journal records what a scene's playback requests got and how it resumed). Demos # scene_manager . play_recording ( path = DEMO_PATH , then = self ) # any key or button returns to `then` A demo plays at the game's speed from the start of the next frame and ends at the recording's end, at the player's first press (consumed: it never reaches then ), at the recording's own quit, or at a divergence (logged at WARNING as demo diverged: ... , then back to then ). A recording that cannot be played (missing, unreadable, another game's, no scene start) is logged at WARNING and nothing starts. Record a demo with scripts/record_scripted_session.py --output PATH (it runs --record-trace , so its first frame holds the scene start). Bundled demos are recordings shipped in the game's package, glitchygames/examples/<game>_demos/<name>.jsonl.gz . PaddleSlap's game-over screen plays rally.jsonl.gz after 10 seconds without a press. tests/replay/test_bundled_demos.py replays every bundled demo headless, so a change that makes a demo diverge fails in CI before it ships. Instant replay # class Match ( Scene ): INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS = 5.0 # opt in: show the last 5 seconds MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS = 60.0 # the default budget def on_goal ( self ): self . scene_manager . instant_replay () # False (logged) when it cannot play A scene class that sets INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS keeps, in memory, the recording of every frame since its first logic frame ( glitchygames/instant_replay.py ), sprites included: about 0.5 MB per minute for one sprite moving every frame, about 1.5 MB per minute for PaddleSlap. The journal ends when another scene is presented, and once it holds more frame time than MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS (paused frames count: all are re-simulated), after which instant_replay() returns False ; longer scenes would need state snapshots. instant_replay() rebuilds the scene from its start, runs the frames before the last INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time unseen, unpaced and silent, shows the rest at the game's pace with their sounds, then the live scene goes on exactly where it was. The player's presses do not end it. To let the player skip it, read the player's input in a supervisor and end the playback there ( end_playback() is honoured only from a supervisor or between frames): class SkipReplayOnPress : def on_frame ( self , * , frame_number , scene ): player_input = scene_manager . playback_player_input # None outside a playback if player_input is not None and player_input . key_pressed ( pygame . K_SPACE ): scene_manager . end_playback () Instant replays can follow one another (a replay after every goal): a playback suspends the journal, which resumes afterwards, and a request the scene's own code makes while its journal plays back gets the answer it got live. Ghosts # A ghost is a recorded sprite's path and looks drawn beside live play, a time-trial ghost ( glitchygames/replay/ghosts.py 's docstring is the contract). Ghosts are appearance, not play: they have no hitbox and change nothing the game does. from glitchygames.replay.ghosts import ( GhostRecorder , GhostSprite , GhostTrack , images_from_animated_sprite , ) # Recording: from the scene's start until the lap ends recorder = GhostRecorder ( sprite = self . player , scene = self ) ... track = recorder . finish () saves . save ( 'best_lap' , track . to_json ()) # Playing it in the next run of the scene (in setup()) track = GhostTrack . from_json ( saves . load ( 'best_lap' )) ghost = GhostSprite ( track = track , image_for = images_from_animated_sprite ( self . player )) ghost . scene = self # the ghost follows this scene's game_time self . all_sprites . add ( ghost ) # never to a collision group GhostRecorder is a supervisor: once per frame, after the frame's logic, it samples the scene's game_time , the sprite's world_x / world_y , its appearance (animation, frame, horizontal flip and draw offset of an AnimatedSprite ; pass appearance= for anything else) and whether the game shows it ( not hidden ). It samples only live frames of the scene it was given, and only when that scene's game time advanced: not behind the pause screen, not in a demo or instant replay. It reads game state only, so recording a ghost changes nothing. Supervisors added while a demo or instant replay plays belong to that playback and are removed when it ends, so a recorder the rebuilt scene's setup() makes never outlives it. Samples are keyed by Scene.game_time , which stops while the scene is paused. The ghost shows the last sample not after the current game_time , so it lines up with the live run from the scene's start at any frame rate, and waits while the game is paused. GhostSprite is a world-space sprite: the engine positions and culls it. Its position is read from the track whenever the engine reads it, so it is drawn in this frame's place, not last frame's. Its image is image_for(sample) drawn translucent ( alpha , default 96). Hide it with ghost.hidden = True (the game's own flag, as for every world sprite). With nothing to show (before the track's first sample, or a sample the game had hidden) its image is empty, so the engine culls it. A ghost in all_sprites is in a recording's sprite trace like any sprite. Store tracks in saves: a replay serves the saves the recording saw, so a session with a ghost replays exactly.
docs.title: Gameplay Recording and Replay

docs.text: GlitchyGames can record a play session and replay it exactly through the real engine. Same engine version and same recording give bit-identical sprite traces: every frame's sprite rect and visible match the recording. Audio is played during a replay but is not compared. This page covers recording, exact replay, watching a replay (with step back and bookmarks), headless runs, the determinism audit, golden replays and rebaselining them, in-game playback (demos, instant replay, ghosts), and the rules game code follows so its sessions replay. See plans/2026-10-19-gameplay-replay.md for the design and plans/future-work.md for the follow-ups.
docs.title: Gameplay Recording and Replay

docs.text: # Record a session uv run paddleslap --record-trace session.jsonl.gz # Watch it replay exactly, comparing every frame with the recording (press Space to start) uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz # The same with no window, no sound and no pacing; the report goes to stdout, and the exit # code says whether it matched (0) or diverged (1) uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --headless # Check that it replays the same way twice, in fresh processes with different hash seeds uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --audit # After an intentional change: replay the same inputs on the current code, write what it does # to a new recording and print what changed uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --rebaseline new-session.jsonl.gz --headless # Did the code get slower? Compare this machine's processing time per frame with the # recording's; with a limit, more than 10% slower exits 8 uv run paddleslap --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --headless --max-processing-slowdown 10
docs.title: Quick start

docs.text: The engine takes everything from the outside world through a small set of doors , and game code reaches them only through the engine. Live play plugs live providers into the doors; replay plugs in providers that serve the recording. The game cannot tell which one it is talking to, so a replay runs the real engine and the real game code again. Door Live ( LiveSources ) Replay ( ReplaySources ) Event pump pygame's queue recorded batch N for pump call N Frame time the measured start-to-start time the recorded dt Polled input captured from pygame once per frame the recorded snapshot Devices real joysticks and controllers stand-ins built from the recording Saves files on disk ( DiskSaveManager ) in memory ( MemorySaveManager ), seeded from the recording Wall clock the real time the recording's start time plus the frame clock Random seed --random-seed or 64 random bits the recorded seed Pacing the target FPS the target FPS; none under --headless The modules: glitchygames/sources.py : the EngineSources protocol and the registry ( active_sources() , install_sources(sources=...) , reset_sources() ) and the frame clock. It is a leaf module with no engine imports, which avoids an import cycle between the engine and the scenes. install_sources is allowed only before the first frame, so a run never mixes live and recorded input. glitchygames/live_sources.py : LiveSources . glitchygames/recording.py : RecordingSources , which wraps the live doors under --record-trace and records what passes through them. glitchygames/replay/driver.py : ReplaySources , the comparison and the divergence report. tests/test_engine_doors.py scans the package and fails if anything outside the doors reads the raw clock, polls pygame's keyboard or mouse, reads or posts pygame events directly, or enumerates or opens joysticks and controllers. Its ALLOWED_BYPASSES lists the few exceptions, each with its reason.
docs.title: The doors

docs.text: Read time from glitchygames/clock.py or Scene.game_time , never from time , datetime or pygame.time : Use For Scene.game_time gameplay timers and cooldowns; stops while the scene is paused frame_clock_seconds() , frame_clock_milliseconds() blinks, animation, "how long since" in UI; never pauses wall_clock_time() , wall_clock_epoch_seconds() timestamps (save metadata, undo history, logs) elapsed_seconds() throttles, debounces, repeat intervals, timeouts (subtract two readings) measured_seconds() real durations for logs and metrics only elapsed_seconds() is the frame clock, live and in a replay, so a throttle near its threshold decides the same way both times; such timers advance once per frame. In a recorded run (and its replay) wall_clock_time() is the recording's start time ( recorded_at ) plus the frame clock, so a timestamp the game shows replays exactly; live play without recording reads the real wall clock. measured_seconds() is real monotonic time and is never replayed: never let its value change what is drawn, played or recorded. Text-widget cursor blinks use the frame clock, not Scene.game_time . A paused scene's widgets are neither updated nor drawn, so a blink cannot be seen advancing while the game is paused.
docs.title: Time

docs.text: Read held keys, modifiers, the mouse and device positions from the frame's input snapshot, never from pygame: from glitchygames.input.state import current_input snapshot = current_input () # or GameEngine.input snapshot . key_pressed ( pygame . K_LEFT ) # by key code (follows the layout) snapshot . scancode_pressed ( scancode = pygame . KSCAN_W ) # by physical position (every layout) snapshot . modifiers # KMOD bits snapshot . mouse_position # (x, y) snapshot . mouse_buttons # (left, middle, right) snapshot . axis ( device_id = instance_id , axis = 0 ) # joystick layer, -1.0 .. 1.0 snapshot . button ( device_id = instance_id , button = 3 ) snapshot . hat ( device_id = instance_id , hat = 0 ) snapshot . controller_axis ( device_id = instance_id , axis = pygame . CONTROLLER_AXIS_LEFTX ) # int scale snapshot . controller_button ( device_id = instance_id , button = pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_A ) The snapshot is immutable and is taken once per frame, right after the frame's first event pump. dt_tick runs before the pump, so there it is the previous frame's snapshot (the same lag as polling pygame had). Devices are keyed by instance id. A game controller is read on two layers: its joystick view ( axis , button , hat ) and the controller layer ( controller_axis , controller_button ). Held keys are physical positions (scancodes), and a key code depends on the keyboard layout (the key in the A position is K_q on AZERTY). A recording therefore also holds the key codes the held keys had on the recording machine, and a replay answers key_pressed(pygame.K_q) as that machine did, whatever the replaying machine's layout. Only pygame's K_* key codes are recorded. Limitation (BUGS.md #83): keys a layout adds that pygame names no K_* constant for, such as French é , German ß or Spanish ñ (SDL gives them their character's code point as the key code), are not in that list. The recorder can only find the held key codes by trying every K_* constant (pygame lets Python ask a key code's position, not a position's key code), so a game that polls one, say key_pressed(ord('é')) , reads it held live but not held in a replay, even on the machine that recorded it. Key events are unaffected (a recorded KEYDOWN or KEYUP keeps its key , whatever its value), and so are positional controls ( scancode_pressed , ActionMap.bind(scancode=...) ). Handle such keys through events or by position, not by polling their key code. For positional controls (movement, say), poll scancode_pressed(scancode=pygame.KSCAN_*) : no keymap is consulted, so it is the same key on every layout, live or replayed, as ActionMap.bind(scancode=...) is for events.
docs.title: Polled input

docs.text: Enumerate and open joysticks and controllers only through active_sources().devices() ( glitchygames/input/devices.py ): joystick_count() , controller_count() , is_controller(device_index=...) , name_for_index(device_index=...) , open_joystick(device_index=...) , open_controller(device_index=...) and joystick_for_instance(instance_id=...) . A recording stores every answer (failures included) and a descriptor of every opened device. A replay gives the recorded answers and stand-ins ( ReplayJoystick , ReplayController ) whose positions come from the snapshot and whose rumble is dropped, so it never needs the recorded hardware and never sees a device that happens to be plugged in.
docs.title: Devices

docs.text: Open a save store with glitchygames.state.open_saves(app_name=...) . Live play gets a DiskSaveManager . A replay gets a MemorySaveManager seeded from the recording's snapshot of that namespace: reads see what the original session saw, writes stay in memory, and real saves are never touched. Both are SaveManager s, which hold every rule of the save format. A recording's header holds each store as it was first opened, so a first scene whose setup() writes to its saves (adds one to a play count) replays from the saves it found. Slots saved at the same time are listed by name, so list_slots() gives the same order everywhere.
docs.title: Saves

docs.text: Post events with glitchygames.recording.post_event , not pygame.event.post , so a recording can mark them internal. Replay delivers internal events from the code that posts them again; an SDL-type event posted directly would be delivered twice. Code that drives the game from outside its logic, as a player would (a supervisor, a test harness, a tool), posts with glitchygames.recording.post_input_event instead. The event is recorded as external input, whatever its type, so --replay-trace , instant replays and demos serve it whether or not they run the poster again (a copy the replayed code posts is dropped). A supervisor that posts with post_event is taken for the game itself, and a replay that does not run it diverges. Draw random numbers from the seeded named streams in glitchygames/randomness.py ( random_stream('name') , numpy_stream('name') ), never from the global random functions, secrets or an unseeded numpy generator.
docs.title: Events and randomness

docs.text: A supervisor ( glitchygames/supervision.py ) is called once per frame at a fixed place: after logic and events, before frame services, camera aim and positioning. What it changes is drawn that frame and seen by collision on the next one. scene_manager . add_supervisor ( supervisor = my_supervisor ) # my_supervisor.on_frame(frame_number=..., scene=...) scene_manager . add_control_event_handler ( kind = 'breakpoint' , handler = on_breakpoint ) scene_manager . record_control_event ( kind = 'breakpoint' , data = { 'label' : 'ball through paddle' }) A control event is a supervisor action recorded in the frame it happened in. A replay applies the recorded control events again at the same frame's supervisor slot, so sessions with supervisor actions replay exactly. A future cheat device will use this hook and channel.
docs.title: The supervisor hook and control events

docs.text: A recording is a gzip JSON Lines trace (format version 3; versions 2 and 3 can be read): a header line, then exactly one line per main-loop frame. Each frame holds its dt , every event batch the engine read from SDL's queue (each event tagged external or internal ) and the sprites. Format 3 adds per-frame input_changes , control_events , devices_opened , saves_opened , device_enumeration and scene_start (each written only when not empty). The header holds the game, scene and versions, every option, the start time, the random seed, and the saves and devices the run took in before recording started. The full format is described in the glitchygames/recording.py module docstring.
docs.title: Recording (--record-trace PATH)

docs.text: A recording also holds how each scene began, so in-game playback (demos, instant replay) can rebuild a scene from its start: the scene's first logic frame (the first frame whose dt_tick runs on it) carries its scene_start (its class's module and qualified name, so two loaded scenes of the same name are told apart, replay_arguments() , every random stream's state and the frame clock as its __init__ began and again as its first setup() began, the saves as they were before its __init__ ran, and the state its first logic frame began in; glitchygames/scene_start.py ). A playback starts there. Frame 0 holds the first scene's start when the run was started with --record-trace (or --rebaseline ). Starts are captured only while they can be used (recording, playback, or a scene that opts into instant replay), so live play pays nothing. A scene that cannot be rebuilt on its own sets CAPTURES_SCENE_START = False (the pause screen does). A replay never compares starts. A scene built with arguments besides options (Clockwork Keep's next floor carries the score and lives) returns them from replay_arguments() , as they were when it was built; they must read back from JSON exactly as returned: class FloorScene ( Scene ): def __init__ ( self , floor_index = 0 , player_score = 0 , options = None , groups = None ): super () . __init__ ( options = options , groups = groups ) # first: the start capture begins here self . floor_index = floor_index self . starting_player_score = player_score def replay_arguments ( self ): return { 'floor_index' : self . floor_index , 'player_score' : self . starting_player_score } Draw random numbers only after super().__init__() : the capture begins there.
docs.title: Scene starts

docs.text: At startup the replay reads the recording, applies its recorded options and seeds the random streams with its seed. It refuses, logging the reason and exiting with one of the exit codes , when: the recording is of another game, cannot be read (not gzip, no permission, a directory) or has an unsupported format version: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65); the file does not exist: MISSING_INPUT (66); --record-trace is given too: OPTIONS_REFUSED (64). Recording over a replay is what --rebaseline does, and only it. A recording made by a different engine version replays with one warning. A version-2 recording replays with one warning too: it has no input snapshots, so polled input reads as idle. Each frame, the replay serves the recorded events, dt , input, devices, saves and clocks. Then it compares the frame with the recording: the active scene's class, then each recorded sprite in draw order (present, rect , visible ), along with the frame's internal events, control events and pump count. The first difference stops a headless replay, as does the last recorded frame; a watched replay pauses there instead. Closing the window stops any replay. Then it reports how it went (logged, or printed to stdout under --headless ). A sprite divergence lists that sprite in the last 20 frames up to the divergent one, as recorded and as replayed: Replay diverged at frame 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16] Ball#2, last 20 frames (expected | got): 6100: [400, 290, 16, 16] visible | [400, 290, 16, 16] visible ... 6120: [412, 300, 16, 16] visible | [412, 301, 16, 16] visible Other divergences (the scene, an event, the frame or pump count) are reported on their one line. A replay that matched reports Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording) (or (quit before the end) , when the window was closed or a watched replay's viewer pressed Esc), and one that matched up to the cut-off of a truncated recording Replay ended early at frame 4312: the recording is truncated . Every replay that ends normally, watched or headless, exits with its result: SUCCESS (0) when it matched or was quit before the end, REPLAY_DIVERGED (1) when it diverged, UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) for a truncated recording. A crash, Ctrl-C, a signal or the game's own exit ends the run as for any run, and the report then says only where the replay stopped ( Replay stopped at frame 12: the run ended with INTERNAL_ERROR (70) ); if the replay had already reached its result, the report gives it, then then the run ended with ... (see exit codes ). The game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) ) before the replay reached its result exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), never SUCCESS , which would say it matched (a rebaseline takes it as the game ending early instead: below). A recording whose header or first frame cannot be decoded (a malformed device, saves or input field) is refused as unusable ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , 65), like an unreadable file. While a replay runs, real keyboard, mouse, touch, joystick, controller, device and window events are blocked at SDL, so they never reach the game (a watched replay leaves key presses and releases unblocked for its controls, which never pass them on to the game). The block is applied again on every pump (event managers created mid-run allow their types again). Each type's earlier blocked state is restored exactly when the replay ends, normally or after an error. QUIT, the window's close event and custom event types are never blocked, so closing the window still ends the replay. Blocking also refuses posts of those types: game code that fakes input by posting KEYDOWN loses the post, which shows up as a missing internal event divergence. A watched replay leaves KEYDOWN and KEYUP unblocked, so such a post arrives there and matches its recording: a recording of a game that posts keys can match watched and diverge headless (and under --audit ). Recorded window references in events are served as None , as live events of the display window carry.
docs.title: Replay (--replay-trace PATH)

docs.text: A replay without --headless is watched: a read-only game inside a game ( glitchygames/replay/viewer.py ). The outer loop, the replay viewer, owns the window: it ticks 60 times a second of real time whatever the speed and whether paused, reads the viewer's keys, and presents the recorded game's latest frame with the status bar drawn on it. The inner loop, the recorded game, runs its frames in full (logic, update and render) at their recorded frame times: each tick runs as many as the real time since the last tick, times the speed, pays for (at most MAX_INNER_FRAMES_PER_TICK , and only within an 11 ms real-time budget per tick, so keys and drawing keep their 60 Hz). It never owes more than one tick's worth: after a stall it runs one bounded burst and drops the rest, and when the recorded game cannot keep up with the speed the status bar says so and shows the real speed ( can't keep up: ×3.2 ). So 1x shows about one recorded frame per tick, 8x about eight, ¼x one every fourth tick. Which frames run when never changes what they do, so a watched replay is exactly as exact as a headless one. It first runs frame 0, then holds on a start screen: that frame dimmed, "Press Spacebar to Start Game Replay" centred, and a smaller line naming the debug overlay's keys ( F3: debug overlay F4: next panel ). Frame 0's sounds play before Space, and a one-frame recording reaches its end at the start screen. The screen is drawn by the pause screen's MessageScreen ( glitchygames/ui/message_screen.py ) with its own message and look, as an overlay on the presented frame: switching to a real pause scene would change the recorded scene sequence. Nothing runs while the replay is held: no frame, no frame clock, no recorded input. The viewer's keys go to the replay's controls ( glitchygames/replay/controls.py ), never to the game. Each key acts once per press (the key repeat games turn on is ignored); . and , held act once, then after 300 ms ten times a second: Key Action Space Start the replay from the start screen, then pause or resume . While paused, run one frame , While paused, step back one frame (held: one more frame back per repeat, restarting once on release) Home Restart at the beginning, paused after frame 0 D Restart just before the divergence, once the replay has found one ] / [ Double or halve the playback speed (0.25 to 8) B Bookmark the frame shown in the status bar S Save a copy of the recording with the bookmarks as breakpoints Esc Quit the replay F3 / F4 Toggle the debug overlay / show its next panel A status bar at the bottom centre shows frame 6120 / 9800 · 1:42.0 · ×1 · paused · diverged at 6120 (the parts that apply), drawn on the presented frame after the debug overlay, so it is never in a screenshot or a trace. At a divergence or the end of the recording the replay pauses with the debug overlay on and a banner above the status bar ( Diverged at frame 6120: ... or End of recording ); stepping past the end does nothing, and Esc ends the run with the replay's result.
docs.title: Watching a replay

docs.text: With recorded (the default), FPS events, the performance statistics and the debug overlay's performance panel use the recorded frame times, and FPS events are compared exactly. With real , they use this machine's measured frame times and FPS events are not compared; sprites that draw the FPS value may then diverge. Logic always receives the recorded dt .
docs.title: --replay-fps {recorded,real}

docs.text: --headless runs any game on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers: no window and no sound. It sets SDL_VIDEODRIVER and SDL_AUDIODRIVER to dummy as soon as the options are read, before pygame starts its display and mixer. If pygame was already started before the engine (by code run at import), a display or mixer on another driver is restarted on the dummy one, with a warning. A live headless run is paced to the target FPS as usual (an unpaced live frame would last about a millisecond of game time) and ends however the game ends. A headless replay is not paced at all, since its frame times come from the recording, never waits (no start screen, no pause at a divergence or the end; its key events stay blocked), prints its report to stdout instead of logging it, and exits with its result as above.
docs.title: Headless runs (--headless)

docs.text: --replay-trace PATH --audit does not replay in-process. It runs the same command again, with --headless added, as two child processes, with PYTHONHASHSEED set to 1 and 2, and each child writes a SHA-256 digest of every replayed frame. The audit passes (exit SUCCESS , 0) when both runs match the recording and their digests match each other; otherwise it reports the first differing frame and exits AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC (3). A child that cannot start, hangs, crashes (exits with any status but 0, or 1 with a recorded divergence) or writes no digests means the audit could not run: INTERNAL_ERROR (70). Fresh processes and different hash seeds make set and dict ordering bugs show up. The audit compares only what the replay samples: the scene class and each sprite's rect , visible and draw order. Pixels, audio and game state that never moves, hides or reorders a sprite are not compared. It is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) with --replay-fps real , under python -E or -I (which would keep PYTHONHASHSEED from reaching the children) and without --replay-trace . A truncated recording is refused before the children start ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , 65): an audit needs the whole recording.
docs.title: The determinism audit (--audit)

docs.text: The exit code alone says who refused the run and why. Every code is a member of glitchygames.exit_codes.ExitCode (also importable from glitchygames.engine ); the engine logs the code it exits with as Exiting with OPTIONS_REFUSED (64) . Code ExitCode member Meaning 0 SUCCESS Success; the replay matched; the audit is deterministic; the rebaseline was written 1 REPLAY_DIVERGED A replay's frames differ from the recording 2 ARGUMENT_PARSER_ERROR A usage error from argparse; the engine never exits with it itself 3 AUDIT_NONDETERMINISTIC --audit 's two runs differ from each other or from the recording 4 GENERATION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's generation request 5 EXTRACTION_REJECTED The API server rejected the sprite client's frame extraction 6 AUDIO_DROPOUT_RISK scripts/audio_glitch_probe.py found a risk of audio dropouts 7 REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST --rebaseline wrote NEW, but the run never received some of OLD's input (it ended early, or did not pump a recorded batch) 8 PROCESSING_SLOWER A replay matched, but its processing time exceeded the recording's by more than --max-processing-slowdown 64 OPTIONS_REFUSED The engine refuses the options given (a combination it will not run) 65 UNUSABLE_INPUT The recording or input data is unusable (another game's recording, an unsupported format version, a corrupt or unreadable file, a bad server response) 66 MISSING_INPUT The input file does not exist 69 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE A required service (the API server) cannot be reached 70 INTERNAL_ERROR An uncaught exception during a run or its teardown (logged with its traceback, after the teardown), or an audit that could not run 73 CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT An output file or directory cannot be created or written (a rebaseline's new recording could not be moved into place) 129 HANGUP Stopped by SIGHUP (Unix only) 130 INTERRUPTED Stopped by SIGINT (Ctrl-C) 143 TERMINATED Stopped by SIGTERM 149 BREAK Stopped by SIGBREAK (Windows only: Ctrl-Break) 0, 64-70 and 73 have the values of BSD sysexits.h (Python's os.EX_OK , os.EX_USAGE and so on, which exist only on Unix, so the values are defined in the engine). The signal codes are 128 + the signal number. A run stopped by one of those signals exits only after the normal teardown, so a recording is complete: the engine handles SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGBREAK for the whole run (unless the game installed its own handler) and turns off SDL's own signal handling ( SDL_NO_SIGNAL_HANDLERS ), which would otherwise turn SIGINT and SIGTERM into a QUIT event. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, Python ignores SIGPIPE, and SIGQUIT keeps its core-dump convention. An engine started off the main thread cannot install its handlers, so SIGTERM then ends it the system's default way, without the teardown. An exception raised before the run starts (while the engine is being constructed) exits with Python's default status 1.
docs.title: Exit codes

docs.text: A recording holds each frame's processing time ( processing_seconds ): the frame's work (logic, events, frame services, positioning and rendering), without presenting it, without the recorder's own writing and without the pacing sleep. The header's latest measurement run ( measurement_runs[0] , see "Content hashes and measurement history" below) names the machine it was measured on (system, version and architecture, never the host name). These are diagnostics: a replay never compares them with the recording to decide whether it matched, and never serves them to the game. The comparison uses the newest entry, processing_seconds[0] . --replay-trace PATH --headless --compare-processing measures this machine's processing time for every replayed frame the same way and prints one line after the replay's report: Replay matched 9800 frames (end of recording) Processing: the replay took 14.2% longer than the recording (9800 frames: 30.410 s against 26.630 s; median frame 3.100 ms against 2.710 ms); slowest against the recording: frame 812 +6.100 ms, frame 813 +5.920 ms, frame 4400 +3.010 ms --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT (which implies --compare-processing ) makes it a check: a replay that matched but took more than PERCENT longer in total exits PROCESSING_SLOWER (8). A divergence still exits REPLAY_DIVERGED (1), and a recording without processing times (made before they were recorded) cannot be checked: UNUSABLE_INPUT (65), with Processing: nothing to compare after the report. Why processing time and not wall-clock time: a live run is paced (most of each frame is the sleep before the next) and a headless replay is not paced at all, so their total times measure different things. Processing time measures the same work in both. It only compares on the same machine, so make the baseline on the machine that will check it (a CI runner); the report says so when the recording names another machine. Pacing still slows the work itself: between paced frames the processor idles and clocks down, so a live recording's frames take longer than the same frames in an unpaced replay (one Clockwork Keep session measured about 65% faster replayed than recorded live). So make the baseline with a rebaseline, which is measured unpaced as every later replay is, and check against it: # Once, on the CI machine: the baseline (the same inputs, measured unpaced) uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace session.jsonl.gz --rebaseline baseline.jsonl.gz --headless # On every change: fail if the work got more than 10% slower uv run clockwork-keep --replay-trace baseline.jsonl.gz --headless --max-processing-slowdown 10 Replays of the same session against such a baseline land within about 1% of it. The latest measurement run says whether it paced its frames ( processing_paced ; a live run with a target FPS, as recording began) and names its frame-pacing timer, paced or not ( pacing_timer : the timer backend, its final spin and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did; glitchygames/timing.py ), and the report adds a note when the baseline was paced. --compare-processing needs --headless (a watched replay presents, steps and rebuilds frames as its viewer asks) and is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) with --audit and with --rebaseline (a rebaseline's NEW records the current code's own processing times anyway). The contract is glitchygames/replay/processing.py 's docstring.
docs.title: Comparing processing time (--compare-processing)

docs.text: Every frame a recorder writes carries two histories, newest first, and the header a third (design: plans/2026-10-20-recording-content-hash-and-history.md ; contract: glitchygames/recording_history.py ): Where Field Each entry Depth constant (10) frame content_hash the frame's content hash CONTENT_HASH_HISTORY_DEPTH frame processing_seconds its processing time ( null when not measured) PROCESSING_SECONDS_HISTORY_DEPTH header measurement_runs the run's provenance: machine, processing_paced , pacing_timer (its frame-pacing timer, paced or not: backend, final spin, and the sleep model --timer-backend auto measured, null if it never did), engine, pygame and Python versions, measured_at , rebaselined_from , hash_scheme , and frame_count (how many frames it wrote; filled in when the next rebaseline stacks onto it, null for the newest run, whose count is the file's) MEASUREMENT_RUNS_HISTORY_DEPTH A fresh recording writes one entry in each. A rebaseline puts its own in front of the replayed recording's and drops the oldest past the depth, so index i means run i in every list. If the runs' depth is tuned below the hash depth, the deeper hashes have no run, so no hash_scheme : treat their scheme as unknown. A reader takes the fields of a run it knows and ignores fields a newer engine added. The content hash is the first 64 bits of SHA-256 of the frame's content fields as a JSON reader decodes them (string keys, lists), encoded as compact, key-sorted JSON (hash scheme 1), so the stored hash is the one a reader recomputes from the frame it reads. Content is everything the game did or took in: dt , the event batches, input, control events, devices, saves, scene starts, the scene and its sprites. Measurements (the two history fields) are left out. Every frame field is one or the other, and the hash refuses a field that is neither, so a new field cannot slip in or out unnoticed. A rebaseline copies the inputs, dt included, so an unchanged game gives the same hash one entry deeper, and a changed one shows exactly which frames changed. Two fresh recordings of the same script differ anyway (each measures its own dt , and the game moves by it). A recording's own hash, for any run, is derived from its frames' hashes: recording_content_hash(frames=..., run_index=i) ; it is not stored. Neither history is compared by a replay or served to the game. They are the record the baselines in the repository keep: behaviour (hashes) and speed (processing times) over time.
docs.title: Content hashes and measurement history

docs.text: tests/fixtures/replays/<game>/golden.jsonl.gz holds a recorded session of each example game (PaddleSlap, Clockwork Keep and both Brave Adventurer editions). scripts/record_scripted_session.py recorded them through the real engine loop, with a supervisor posting each game's golden input script. Each recording is a test item of its own: the pytest plugin glitchygames/testing/replays.py (loaded by the root conftest.py ) collects every .../fixtures/replays/<console-script>/<name>.jsonl.gz as <console-script>/<name> , replays it headless in a child process through the console script's entry point ( --replay-trace PATH --headless ) and fails, with the exit code and the child's output (the divergence report), unless it exits ExitCode.SUCCESS . A directory that is not a console script is a collection error. Another project's games can use the plugin the same way ( pytest_plugins = ['glitchygames.testing.replays'] ). Re-record a fixture only deliberately, after finding out why it stopped replaying; the commands are in the script's docstring. After an intentional change, rebaseline it instead (below), so it keeps its recorded inputs.
docs.title: Golden replays

docs.text: --replay-trace OLD --rebaseline NEW --headless replays OLD's inputs on the current code and writes what that code did to NEW: the same inputs and a new picture. The contract is glitchygames/replay/rebaseline.py 's docstring. The replay does not stop at a divergence: it runs to OLD's last frame (or until the game ends), counting every frame that differs and naming every sprite that differs in them. NEW holds OLD's inputs as the replay served them: the event batches with their origins (code-posted events stay internal , so replaying NEW delivers nothing twice), dt , input_changes , re-applied control events, and each frame's saves_opened , devices_opened and device_enumeration copied from OLD. Its sprites and markers are the current code's. Its header is OLD's (seed, start time, options, saves, devices) with rebaselined_from naming OLD and this run's engine, pygame and Python versions. A cut-off (truncated) OLD gives NEW source_truncated : NEW ends as truncated too, so its replay exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) at the cut-off, --audit refuses it, and it cannot be a golden fixture (the plugin expects SUCCESS ). Rebaseline a complete recording for those. A version-2 OLD (no input snapshots) gives an honest format-3 NEW: its polled input is the idle input the replay served, recorded as such, and its markers are compared when NEW is replayed (OLD's were not). Input OLD has that the run never received is not moved anywhere else (that would invent an input sequence OLD does not have); it is reported. That is the external events of batches a frame did not pump (the current code pumped fewer times than recorded), and OLD's frames after the game ended early. NEW is written to NEW.partial and moved into place only when the run ends normally; a run that crashes, is interrupted or fails its own exit ( sys.exit(1) ) writes nothing; the game's own successful exit ( sys.exit(0) ) ends it early as quit_game() does (NEW holds the frames that ran, exit REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST ). If the move fails (say NEW is a directory), the finished NEW.partial is kept, its path logged and printed, and the run exits CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73). NEW is never OLD, and NEW.partial is never OLD either. A NEW.partial that cannot be written at all is refused before the replay starts, with one line and CANNOT_WRITE_OUTPUT (73), as is an unwritable --record-trace or --replay-digest file. NEW is an original, never a bookmarked copy (OLD's bookmarked_copy_of is dropped), so S on a replay of NEW never rewrites it. It prints one line to stdout and exits SUCCESS (0), however many frames differ: Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: 412 frames differ (first at 6120: sprite Ball#2 rect expected [412, 300, 16, 16], got [412, 301, 16, 16]); sprites affected: Ball#2, Ball#3 or Rebaselined 9800 frames to NEW: no frames differ . Lost input (above) is added to the line and logged as a warning, e.g. ; 3 recorded input events not delivered (first at frame 812); ended at frame 500 of 9800 . NEW is still written (it replays clean), but the run exits REBASELINE_INPUT_LOST (7) instead, so a script that replaces fixtures notices that NEW is not a faithful re-run of OLD's session. It is refused ( OPTIONS_REFUSED , 64) without --replay-trace or without --headless (a watched replay holds frames and takes the viewer's keys, so it is refused rather than made headless quietly), when NEW or NEW.partial is OLD's file, and with --record-trace , --audit , --replay-digest (the audit's tools; a rebaseline is not audited) or --replay-fps real (FPS events from this machine's frame times would become the baseline). An unusable OLD is refused like any replay ( UNUSABLE_INPUT , MISSING_INPUT ). NEW replays on the current code with no divergence when the rebaseline replayed all of OLD: a truncated OLD gives a truncated NEW, whose replay matches up to its cut-off and exits UNUSABLE_INPUT (65) like any truncated recording. Replacing a golden fixture with it stays a deliberate, reviewed step: read the summary, check the change is the intended one, then move NEW over the fixture yourself.
docs.title: Rebaselining (--rebaseline NEW)

docs.text: A running game can play a recording to a rebuilt scene and then go on: attract-mode demos, instant replays and ghosts. Demos and instant replays run in a playback scope , not a new engine run ( glitchygames/replay/playback.py 's docstring is the contract): the scene is rebuilt from its start (see Scene starts above) on scoped doors that serve the recording, the live scene is stashed untouched, saves are a sandbox, the random streams, clocks and FPS timer are put back afterwards, and the live game's own posts and the player's releases, device and window events are held and handed back when the scope ends. A --record-trace session that plays a scope records it, and replays it exactly. An error inside the scope ends the scope (logged) and the live game goes on. scene_manager.last_playback_outcome says how the last scope ended (its kind, reason and frames played). What belongs to the scope ends with it: supervisors and control event handlers its scene adds (in setup() , cleanup() or an event handler; a live supervisor's additions stay), and the playback scene's own events still queued when it ends (posted in update() or an event handler after its last pump: the live game never receives them, so a goal posted there cannot start a second instant replay). What the live game's own supervisors and handlers post while it plays stays the live game's: a supervisor that calls end_playback() and then posts an event has it delivered to the live game after the scope. A playback never rumbles the player's controllers, and the live scene's synth voices (and those of the game behind a pause screen the instant replay began from) pause behind it and play on after. Inside a scope, a replay of the session still applies the session's breakpoints (a bookmark on a frame a demo played pauses there); the played recording's own breakpoints are never applied again. A --record-trace recording of a session that played a scope replays exactly, but cannot itself be played in-game from a frame inside or after that scope (only an instant-replay journal records what a scene's playback requests got and how it resumed).
docs.title: In-game playback

docs.text: scene_manager . play_recording ( path = DEMO_PATH , then = self ) # any key or button returns to `then` A demo plays at the game's speed from the start of the next frame and ends at the recording's end, at the player's first press (consumed: it never reaches then ), at the recording's own quit, or at a divergence (logged at WARNING as demo diverged: ... , then back to then ). A recording that cannot be played (missing, unreadable, another game's, no scene start) is logged at WARNING and nothing starts. Record a demo with scripts/record_scripted_session.py --output PATH (it runs --record-trace , so its first frame holds the scene start). Bundled demos are recordings shipped in the game's package, glitchygames/examples/<game>_demos/<name>.jsonl.gz . PaddleSlap's game-over screen plays rally.jsonl.gz after 10 seconds without a press. tests/replay/test_bundled_demos.py replays every bundled demo headless, so a change that makes a demo diverge fails in CI before it ships.
docs.title: Demos

docs.text: class Match ( Scene ): INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS = 5.0 # opt in: show the last 5 seconds MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS = 60.0 # the default budget def on_goal ( self ): self . scene_manager . instant_replay () # False (logged) when it cannot play A scene class that sets INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS keeps, in memory, the recording of every frame since its first logic frame ( glitchygames/instant_replay.py ), sprites included: about 0.5 MB per minute for one sprite moving every frame, about 1.5 MB per minute for PaddleSlap. The journal ends when another scene is presented, and once it holds more frame time than MAX_INSTANT_REPLAY_FAST_FORWARD_SECONDS (paused frames count: all are re-simulated), after which instant_replay() returns False ; longer scenes would need state snapshots. instant_replay() rebuilds the scene from its start, runs the frames before the last INSTANT_REPLAY_SECONDS of frame time unseen, unpaced and silent, shows the rest at the game's pace with their sounds, then the live scene goes on exactly where it was. The player's presses do not end it. To let the player skip it, read the player's input in a supervisor and end the playback there ( end_playback() is honoured only from a supervisor or between frames): class SkipReplayOnPress : def on_frame ( self , * , frame_number , scene ): player_input = scene_manager . playback_player_input # None outside a playback if player_input is not None and player_input . key_pressed ( pygame . K_SPACE ): scene_manager . end_playback () Instant replays can follow one another (a replay after every goal): a playback suspends the journal, which resumes afterwards, and a request the scene's own code makes while its journal plays back gets the answer it got live.
docs.title: Instant replay

docs.text: A ghost is a recorded sprite's path and looks drawn beside live play, a time-trial ghost ( glitchygames/replay/ghosts.py 's docstring is the contract). Ghosts are appearance, not play: they have no hitbox and change nothing the game does. from glitchygames.replay.ghosts import ( GhostRecorder , GhostSprite , GhostTrack , images_from_animated_sprite , ) # Recording: from the scene's start until the lap ends recorder = GhostRecorder ( sprite = self . player , scene = self ) ... track = recorder . finish () saves . save ( 'best_lap' , track . to_json ()) # Playing it in the next run of the scene (in setup()) track = GhostTrack . from_json ( saves . load ( 'best_lap' )) ghost = GhostSprite ( track = track , image_for = images_from_animated_sprite ( self . player )) ghost . scene = self # the ghost follows this scene's game_time self . all_sprites . add ( ghost ) # never to a collision group GhostRecorder is a supervisor: once per frame, after the frame's logic, it samples the scene's game_time , the sprite's world_x / world_y , its appearance (animation, frame, horizontal flip and draw offset of an AnimatedSprite ; pass appearance= for anything else) and whether the game shows it ( not hidden ). It samples only live frames of the scene it was given, and only when that scene's game time advanced: not behind the pause screen, not in a demo or instant replay. It reads game state only, so recording a ghost changes nothing. Supervisors added while a demo or instant replay plays belong to that playback and are removed when it ends, so a recorder the rebuilt scene's setup() makes never outlives it. Samples are keyed by Scene.game_time , which stops while the scene is paused. The ghost shows the last sample not after the current game_time , so it lines up with the live run from the scene's start at any frame rate, and waits while the game is paused. GhostSprite is a world-space sprite: the engine positions and culls it. Its position is read from the track whenever the engine reads it, so it is drawn in this frame's place, not last frame's.
